title: Hooks for Real Estate Agents: 40 Openers That Stop the Scroll
markdown:
# Hooks for Real Estate Agents: 40 Openers That Stop the Scroll

At 8:14 a.m., a listing video opens with “Here’s a beautiful home in [ADD: neighborhood]”—and the viewer has already swiped. The first line has to give a buyer, seller, or curious neighbor a reason to stay.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/uO68lfcXhM.png)

This page gives you ready-to-film hooks for real estate agents, plus a simple way to choose and test them. Replace the brackets with facts you can verify about the property, market, or client situation.

## Listing-tour hooks

1. “This [ADD: price] home has one room buyers keep walking back into.”
2. “Before you judge this house from the street, wait until you see the back.”
3. “You can get [ADD: number] bedrooms here without leaving [ADD: neighborhood].”
4. “This is what [ADD: price range] buys in [ADD: neighborhood] today.”
5. “The listing photos missed the best part of this home.”
6. “If a quiet morning matters to you, start with this room.”
7. “This kitchen answers one question: can a family actually use it?”
8. “The first feature buyers notice here is not the fireplace.”
9. “Would you trade [ADD: feature] for this location?”
10. “This home looks ordinary for exactly three seconds.”

## Neighborhood hooks

11. “Want to know what living in [ADD: neighborhood] actually feels like?”
12. “The best reason to consider [ADD: neighborhood] is not the commute.”
13. “Before you move to [ADD: neighborhood], walk this block with me.”
14. “This is the question I would ask before buying near [ADD: landmark].”
15. “A [ADD: property type] in [ADD: neighborhood] can mean two very different lifestyles.”
16. “Here is where locals go when they do not want the obvious option.”
17. “If you need [ADD: priority], this part of [ADD: neighborhood] deserves a look.”
18. “The map says one thing about this neighborhood. A walk through it says another.”
19. “This corner explains why buyers keep asking about [ADD: neighborhood].”
20. “Is [ADD: neighborhood] right for you? Start with this trade-off.”

## First-time buyer hooks

21. “The first number a buyer sees is not the only number that matters.”
22. “Before you book another showing, ask your lender this.”
23. “A lower list price can cost more—here is where to look.”
24. “First-time buyers: do not confuse ‘needs work’ with this.”
25. “The home you can afford and the home you can comfortably keep are not always the same.”
26. “This is the inspection question that can change your next step.”
27. “If you are waiting for the perfect home, define ‘perfect’ first.”
28. “You do not need to know every market term before your first tour.”
29. “Here is how to compare two homes without getting lost in the finishes.”
30. “The offer is not the finish line. It is the start of a new checklist.”

## Seller hooks

31. “Before you list, stand at your front door and look at this.”
32. “A seller asked what to fix first. This was the order.”
33. “Not every update belongs on your pre-listing list.”
34. “Your first showing begins before anyone opens the door.”
35. “The question is not ‘Should I stage?’ It is ‘What must a buyer understand fast?’”
36. “Before you choose a list price, separate these two ideas.”
37. “A clean room and a ready-to-show room are not the same thing.”
38. “The most useful seller prep can take [ADD: time]—if this is the bottleneck.”
39. “If your home has an unusual feature, do not hide it. Frame it.”
40. “The first buyer question your listing should answer is this.”

## How to pick the right hook

Choose the audience before the line. A listing-tour viewer may care about a specific room or price range. A first-time buyer may need a decision clarified. A seller may need to see a practical next step.

Then choose one hook type:

- **Curiosity:** withhold one specific detail, then reveal it in the video.
- **Question:** name the decision the viewer is already weighing.
- **Contrast:** put two real options or trade-offs side by side.
- **Mistake:** identify a common assumption and explain the better check.
- **Specificity:** use a verified property fact, location, or constraint.

Do not make the hook carry the whole video. The next sentence should immediately prove that the opening was worth hearing. If you say a room changes the home, show the room. If you raise a buyer question, answer it before moving on.

## How to test hooks without guessing

Film the same useful video around one clear subject: a kitchen, a neighborhood walk, a seller-prep task, or a buyer decision. Create two or three opening versions, keeping the footage and core explanation as similar as possible.

Review the result for more than a single score. Look for comments that show the hook drew the intended audience, saves that suggest the advice was useful, and whether viewers reach the explanation after the opener. Keep the version that attracts the right question—not simply the broadest reaction.

A practical test log can be short: topic, audience, hook type, spoken first line, on-screen text, and what viewers asked. After several posts, you will see which openings fit your market and your voice.

## FAQ

### Should real estate agents use the same hook on every video?

No. Use a consistent point of view, but match the opening to the viewer’s job. A buyer comparing homes needs a different first line from a seller preparing to list.

### How long should the spoken hook be?

Keep it short enough to say clearly before the video moves into proof. A single sentence is often enough when it names one specific promise.

### Can I use a hook if I do not have a statistic?

Yes. Use an observable detail, a real trade-off, or a question your audience genuinely asks. Do not add a number you cannot verify.

### What should appear on screen?

Put the core idea in fewer words than you say aloud. For example, spoken: “Before you judge this house from the street, wait until you see the back.” On-screen: “Wait for the backyard.”

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the format it returns:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
